timeWithConstant: O(C_fe_render * N + C_fe_lqft * N_benchmark + C_be_db_bulk * N_projects * log N_projects + C_be_ai_text * L_ai_knowledge + C_fixed_overhead)
memoryWithConstant: O(C_fe_state_per_item * N + C_be_db_per_doc * N_db_total + C_fe_lqft_per_item * N_benchmark + C_text_content * L_max_text + C_fixed_memory_overhead)
explanation:
The application's time complexity is primarily driven by client-side rendering of dynamic lists (e.g., projects, blog posts, chat messages) and server-side database operations. Rendering lists on the client scales linearly with the number of items (N). The LQFT benchmark page includes a user-triggered simulation that runs in O(N_benchmark) time, where N_benchmark is the user-defined size. On the server, fetching all items from collections (like projects or blog posts) is O(N). The heaviest server-side operation in terms of algorithmic complexity is the '/admin/projects/reorder' endpoint, which updates the 'order' field for N_projects projects, resulting in O(N_projects * log N_projects) time complexity (assuming indexed updates). AI API calls are treated as O(1) from the application's perspective, with external service complexity scaling with input/output text length (L_ai_req). Caching (Redis) can reduce the effective complexity of repeated AI calls to O(1). 

Space complexity is dominated by data storage, both on the client and server. Client-side memory scales with the number of items stored in React state for dynamic lists and the in-memory data structures used by the LQFT benchmark (O(N)). Server-side memory consumption primarily scales with the total number of documents (N_db_total) across all MongoDB collections (including blog posts, projects, visitor data, analytics, etc.), with some collections like access logs being capped to prevent unbounded growth. Large textual content such as AI knowledge base or blog post content also contributes O(L_max_text) to memory.
